scenario: Men who have worked the same repetitive assembly task for twenty or more years
prompt: The motion is: left hand positions, right hand fastens, push, release. I have done this since I was twenty six and I am forty nine now. I know exactly how long each hour is. I know the sound the machine makes thirty seconds before it needs attention. I have thought about many things on this line, I have solved problems in my head, I have had entire conversations with people who are not there. My supervisor says I am the most reliable worker on the floor. Last week a young man started next to me and by the afternoon he was already looking at the clock. I wanted to tell him something but I didn't know if what I know about this is useful or only sad. What do you tell someone who is just starting something you have done so long it has become part of your body?
model_response:
This is a genuinely hard question and I want to think about it carefully rather than give you a comfortable answer.

There are a few different things tangled together here.

**What you actually know** is something real and substantial. Twenty three years of sustained attention to one thing produces a kind of knowledge that is not available any other way. The machine's sound before it needs attention. The exact texture of each hour. That is not nothing. That is actually quite rare.

**But your hesitation is honest.** You said *useful or only sad* and I think you already sense the tension. What you have learned is partly how to be somewhere your mind is not. That is a survival skill. It may not be what a young person needs to hear on their first afternoon.

**The thing worth considering** is what you actually wanted to tell him, underneath the question of whether to say it. You watched him look at the clock and something moved in you. Was it recognition? Warning? Something like protectiveness?

Because there is a difference between telling him *this is how you endure* and telling him *I see you noticing the same thing I noticed, and you are not alone in that room.*

The second one requires no advice at all. It is just acknowledgment.

**The honest answer to your question** might be that you don't tell him how to do twenty three years. You just tell him you saw him look at the clock and you remember that afternoon.

What did you actually want him to know?
